creator: Sabine Hossenfelder
title: The Fermi Paradox Just Got Much Worse
full_text:
The Fermi paradox just got so much
worse. One of the most plausible
explanations for why we've not yet heard
of other intelligent species has been
that technological civilizations
eventually develop artificial
intelligence systems and it's not
intelligent to populate the galaxy. They
lose interest basically. But in a new
paper, a physicist now argues quite
convincingly I think that this is wrong.
This isn't just interesting because of
the Fermi paradox, but because it
generally tells us how our attitude to
space travel has been changing. The
Fermi paradox is the question of why we
haven't yet found aliens. The Milky Way
has hundreds of billions of stars. We
now know that planets are common and
that many planets are quite plausibly in
the habitable zones of their stars.
Indeed, many of those planets should
have formed billions of years before
Earth. So, why haven't we heard of any
other intelligent species? Other
civilization should have had plenty of
time to spread through the galaxy, build
visible technology, or at least leave
traces. But we haven't heard or seen
anything from anyone. There have been
lots of different explanations. For
example, that the emergence of life is
just incredibly unlikely or that
habitable planets are much rarer than we
think. But one of the explanations
that's attracted the most attention is
that advanced civilizations simply lose
interest in space travel because it's on
a basic level dumb. Space travel is
expensive and inefficient. And just
exactly what is the purpose anyway?
Humans currently attempt to travel in
space for irrational reasons, so the
argument goes, because of national
pride, because they believe that more
humans are better than fewer humans, or
because they don't fully realize just
how incredibly large the distances are
between solar systems and how long it
would take us to travel there. But once
a civilization develops artificial
intelligence, they grow out of these
silly ideas, so the argument goes, and
instead they make their life cozy on
their home planet, space traveling in
virtual reality. Populating the galaxy
requires too many resources with little
result and is ultimately not
sustainable. A related argument has it
that civilizations just take it slowly
for some billion billion years because
computation becomes thermodynamically
easier then. Quite the argument seeing
that I can't plan ahead enough to
reliably water the plants. In any case,
I've always found this an interesting
argument because it basically pitches
Elon Musk against himself. It would lead
you to expect that at some point Grok
will begin to argue against SpaceX.
Okay, but now here comes the new paper.
The author argues that this earlier
argument is fundamentally flawed. He
says that once a civilization has
artificial intelligence, robots, and
space factories, space exploration
doesn't require big and fast machines.
It can be done with plenty of small,
cheap spacecraft and with machines that
need neither food nor air nor
motivational posters. And that just
makes the Fermi paradox so much worse
because now you have to ask not just,
"Well, why haven't we received any
electromagnetic signal from the aliens?"
but why have we not found any of their
space probes? Why are they not here? The
author gives multiple reasons for why
space exploration is rational, most
importantly the preservation of the
species and possibly other species,
knowledge preservation, and scientific
observation. If the cost of small probes
is small compared with the value of
these factors, then it makes sense. The
author then also offers some estimates
to show how his argument makes the Fermi
paradox worse. He considers a 10 kg seed
probe traveling at 0.01 times the speed
of light. At that speed, it crosses 100
light-years in about 10,000 years and
the galactic disc in about 10 million
years. That's less than 1/10 of 1% of
the age of the galaxy. This means that
any civilization which has developed
such technology should have spread their
probes throughout the galaxy by now.
Okay, but wait, this means there is
another plausible explanation now for
why we haven't heard of those
extraterrestrials.
We've simply looked for the wrong thing.
So far, almost all searches for techno
signatures have been to look for
electromagnetic signals in one way or
another because the aliens would
directly send signals or because they
built structures around their star to
extract energy and thereby dim it or
similar. Maybe we should instead make
more effort to look for alien probes in
the solar system. Maybe some of those
supposed asteroids are not asteroids.
Maybe some of those supposed meteoroids
are not meteoroids. Maybe some of those
unidentified anomalous phenomena are not
camera glitches. I think these are
possibilities that we should take more
seriously. That said, I give this paper
a 10 out of 10 on the meter,
not because it's bad or wrong, but
because I think this isn't actually a
scientific paper. It's more of a
cultural speculation. But it's still
interesting and I think it's another
sign for how much the conversation about
extraterrestrials has changed in the
past decade.

Hi, Elon.
Yeah, it's totally possible that aliens
are here already.
Well, I guess the first thing that I do
would be to get super rich and start a
space travel company and build AI and
robots. Oh,
wait. I read a lot of news every day and
that used to be really tedious because a
lot of headlines repeat and it's
difficult to tell what quality the

much better. Ground News is a news

through a dozen headlines on the same
story. I can just get a quick summary
and fact check for all the coverage. And
Ground News also gives you a lot of
extra information at one glance. An
interesting recent example is the news
when pieces of a space X rocket crashed
into the moon. You can see at one glance
that this was basically a center-right
story with little interest on the
political left. Ground News also gives
you a bias comparison. Left-leaning
coverage stresses disappointed
investors, whereas right-leaning
coverage turns it into a spectacle and
critique. Ground News also gives you a
fact check for each news item, tells you
who owns the media outlets, and that in
this case sources are mostly out of the
UK. Ground News also has this
interesting feature called blind spot.
This collects news which has been
covered only on one side of the
political spectrum. I found Ground News
super useful for putting news into
context quickly. And of course, I have a
special offer for you. That's a 40%
discount on the Vantage plan, which
gives you access to all the features.
All you need to do is use my link
ground.news/sabina
or use the QR code so they'll know I
sent you. Thanks for watching. See you
tomorrow.
